title: Linux Foundation LFCS
summary: The Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator (LFCS) is a performance-based certification that validates a candidate's ability to operate, configure and troubleshoot a live Linux system rather than recall facts about one. It is aimed at working system administrators, DevOps engineers, site reliability engineers and security practitioners who already touch Linux hosts daily and need an externally recognised proof of operational competence, not at beginners looking for a first introduction to the command line. For an employer the credential signals that the holder can be handed a shell on a production server and trusted to manage storage, services, networking, users and permissions without hand-holding, and that they can diagnose a broken system under time pressure. The exam is entirely practical: candidates work inside a real environment and complete a series of hands-on tasks against one or more live systems, with access to documentation during the session, and results depend on the observable state of the machine rather than on multiple-choice recall. Because the environment is real, partial credit is unusual; a service that does not actually start or a mount that does not persist after reboot is simply wrong. That is why lab practice changes outcomes so dramatically. Reading about systemd units, LVM, firewalling or SELinux contexts produces recognition, while repeatedly breaking and repairing a throwaway virtual machine produces the muscle memory the exam actually measures. Practitioners who rehearse on disposable VMs, script their own verification checks and learn to confirm every change from a second shell consistently outperform those who only study guides, and the same habits transfer directly to hardening and incident response work on production fleets.
objectives: Essential Commands: navigate the filesystem, manipulate files and text streams, use package management, and work efficiently with shell pipelines and redirection.
Operations Deployment: manage the boot process, kernel parameters and systemd units, schedule recurring work, and keep services running across reboots.
User and Group Management: create and modify accounts and groups, configure sudo delegation, and reason about password ageing and login policy.
Networking: configure interfaces, addresses, routes, hostname resolution and firewall rules, and diagnose connectivity problems from the host itself.
Storage Management: partition and format disks, manage LVM volumes, create and mount filesystems including network filesystems, and persist mounts via fstab.
Service Configuration: deploy and tune common server roles such as web, database, DNS, file sharing and time synchronisation, and validate them locally.
Security and Access Control: apply file permissions, ACLs and special bits, configure SELinux or AppArmor modes, and manage SSH access and key material.
Scripting and Automation: write shell scripts that accept arguments, test conditions, loop safely and exit with meaningful status codes for automation to consume.
Troubleshooting: read system and service logs, isolate failures in boot, networking, storage and permissions, and restore a working state without a reboot where possible.
